newsitem.title: USA: Bear Stearns sets $4.5 bln rate swap for LIPA pact.
newsitem.headline: Bear Stearns sets $4.5 bln rate swap for LIPA pact.

text.p: Bear Stearns, the financial advisor for the Long Island Power Authority (LIPA), on Tuesday said it set a $4.5 billion interest rate swap option to fix the costs of a huge, proposed sale of tax-exempt bonds.
LIPA plans to sell nearly $7.3 billion of debt to help pay for a partial state takeover of the Long Island Lighting Co, which is merging with Brooklyn Union Gas.

"We think it is the largest hedge transaction of its kind ever done," said Bob Foran, a senior managing director at Bear, Stearns. He explained the swap was awarded in five tranches of $900 million each.
Each tranche was offered at approximately 30-minute intervals. "Then we announced the winning bid and cover, so people could see what the targets were," Foran added.

Under the swap, the winning firms agreed to pay the LIPA-LILCO-Brooklyn Union partnership the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR), while the partnership will pay a fixed-rate. The swaps rates in the five tranches range from 7.557 percent to 7.61 percent.

The hedge, which has a 15-month maturity and can be exercized starting in the 12th month, was won by four firms, Societe Generale, Swiss Bank, Morgan Guaranty, which won the third and fourth tranches, and Chase Manhattan.
Thirteen firms bid for the hedge.
Foran explained that the amount of the hedge was based on the notional amount--approximately 90 percent--of the nearly $7.3 billion sale of tax-exempt debt.

The items that were subtracted included about $1 billion of variable rate debt, $700 million of LILCO debt that will not need to be immediately refinanced and $600 million of debt service reserve-related bonds.
LIPA expects to assume a total of around $3.7 billion of LILCO's debt.

A LILCO spokeswoman said the recent drop in fixed income yields prompted the swap transaction. The interest rate swap provides LIPA with protection if interest rates rise above the 6.7 percent level assumed in its planning. However, the LIPA pact still faces various state and federal regulatory hurdles.
LILCO's taxable bonds rose five to fifteen basis points on the news, traders said.

"This is a vote of confidence in the transaction and the prospects for the deal being consumated. It makes sense the bonds would tighten," said John Spellman, utilities debt analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Traders noted the company's debentures outperformed the gains in other LILCO bonds as investors speculated they were more likely to be assumed by LIPA under the pact. "The debentures are where you want to be," said one trader. "There is a decent shot that the (new LIPA) will tender them and refinance them with lower-cost municipal debt," he added.
